newsitem.title: UK: Dollar closes mixed in European trading, edges lower on yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes mixed in European trading, edges lower on yen.

text.p: The dollar closed mixed in European trading, edging lower against the yen but holding on to some of its gains against the mark.

The much-awaited U.S. employment report for October provided nothing more but a short-lived nudge higher for the dollar since non-farm payrolls rose almost in line with expectations and hourly earnings, a measure of wage inflation, were flat.

"There wasn't much in those numbers to push the dollar either way," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "The most realistic assumption is that the FOMC will stay put on rates when it next meets on November 13."
At 1625 GMT the dollar was at 1.5170/80 marks and 113.37/42 yen, against 1.5128/38 and 113.77/87 in late Europe on Thursday.

Non-farm payrolls rose 210,000 in Ocober against average market expectations for a 212,000 rise. The jobless rate stayed at 5.2 percent.The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index of manufacturing activity fell to 50.2 from 51.7.

Dollar/yen got hit in late trade by a comment from former U.S. Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen who told Reuters Financial Television he would prefer the dollar not to strengthen further against the yen as this would hurt U.S. competetiveness. Bentsen said the dollar was now at a "comfortable level" versus the yen.
Bentsen triggered a sharp decline of the dollar against the yen 2-1/2 years ago by saying he would prefer a lower dollar/yen rate. The dollar was at similar levels then.
Bentsen does not hold an official position now however, and his remarks are contrary to stated U.S. policy, analysts noted.

The key cross to watch next week wil be mark/yen, which once again was a prime mover after an overnight slide. The German unit fell in Tokyo after Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said a strong yen against the mark would help German exporters.
Speculation that the worst of yen weakness might be over has started to weigh on mark/yen, dealers said.

Sterling also grabbed attention, hitting a fresh 2 1/2 year high at 2.4962 before easing back to 2.4795/2.4800 on short-term profit-taking. Cable was off its earlier 20-month high at $1.6435, trading at $1.6355/60 in late business.

"Movements in mark/yen and sterling/mark have been manipulating the dollar all week -- it's things that are going through in the crosses that are moving dollar/mark," said Alan Collins, head of technical analysis at Merita Bank in London.
The U.S. presidential election on Tuesday is unlikely to shake the dollar out of its lethargy as a victory of President Bill Clinton looks certain.
"Clinton's re-election looks virtually like a done deal," said Stretch at NatWest. "He's been ahead in the polls for such a long time that the market has fully priced in his victory."

The dollar could lose its composure even if Clinton wins if the Democrats seize control of the House of Representatives, which would prompt market fears of looser U.S. fiscal and trade policy, a potential negative for the dollar.
